The commentary states: "Mahā" means "great. "Pra-jñā" means "supreme wisdom."
*Pāramitā* means the sense of "departure" (*niḥsaraṇa*) and the sense of "arrival" (*prāpti*).

According to the grammatical treatises (*śabdavidyā*), the analysis of the compound is as follows: *pāra* is the high-pitched vowel *ī*, and *ita* means "this shore"; *pāra* means "the other shore. Thus, it signifies departing from this shore and arriving at the other shore.
Riding upon the wisdom of the Great Ultimate, one leaves the near shore of birth and death and reaches the far shore of nirvāṇa, attaining the great nirvāṇa of non-abiding.
"Svāhā" means reaching the far shore of nirvāṇa from this near shore, attaining the great nirvāṇa of non-abiding.
*Svāhā* means "accomplishment," it also means "auspiciousness," it also means "parinirvāṇa," it also means "pacification and augmentation," and it also means "non-abiding."
Now, taking the meaning of non-abiding, it is precisely non-abiding nirvāṇa.
Relying upon this nirvāṇa, one brings benefit and happiness to sentient beings until the end of the future, without limit; therefore, it is called *svāhā*.
Regarding the aforementioned term "seed" (*bīja*), it carries two meanings:
first, the sense of "drawing forth" (*ākṣepa*); second, the sense of "sustaining" (*dhāraṇa*).

For example, when ten characters form a single phrase, the first character serves as the seed; all the contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) pertaining to the remaining nine characters arises based upon that initial one.
Furthermore, the nine lower characters are subsumed within the first character; that is, the first character sustains and encompasses the remaining nine.
From this it follows that if one knows a single dharma, one knows all dharmas; if one knows the emptiness of a single dharma, one knows the emptiness of all dharmas.

If one can focus one's attention on a single syllable to observe and cultivate all practices and vows, all such practices and vows will be brought to fulfillment; this is because it carries the meaning of *dhāraṇī*, or total retention.

Furthermore, regarding the distinctions in meaning beyond this: the preceding extended practice is subsumed into sixteen phrases; the sixteen phrases are subsumed into twelve characters; the twelve characters are subsumed into ten characters; and those ten characters are subsumed into the single character "Earth" (地). From the broad to the concise, it becomes progressively profound until the single character manifests before one, pervading the entire Dharma-realm; its nature and characteristics are equal, reaching the ultimate stage.
The sequence of the contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) has been extensively analyzed in a separate ritual manual (*vidhi*).
Following this, the third section is the World-Honored One’s seal of approval (*anumodana*), as stated in the Sūtra:
At that time, having heard these words, the World-Honored One praised Vajrapāṇi and the other bodhisattvas, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!

If there are those who recite and uphold this dhāraṇī, I and all the Buddhas of the ten directions shall constantly provide them with protection. All malevolent spirits and deities will revere them as they would a Buddha, and before long they shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
The commentary says:
"Excellent, excellent! For that which was spoken by the Seal (Mudrā) is protected by all Buddhas, out of their reverence for the Mother."
The spirits and deities revere it because of the majestic power of the Dharma;
they shall attain Bodhi and obtain the supreme fruit.
This is the third benefit for all kings.
This section is divided into three parts;
first, the initial section designates the various kings.
The Sūtra states:

“Great King! I entrust this sūtra to you and to all the kings of the following lands: the kingdom of Vaiśālī, the kingdom of Kośala, the kingdom of Śrāvastī, the kingdom of Magadha, the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, the kingdom of Kapilavastu, the kingdom of Kuśinagara, the kingdom of Kauśāmbī, the kingdom of Pañcāla, the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra, the kingdom of Mathurā, the kingdom of Oḍḍiyāna, the kingdom of Puṇḍravardhana, the kingdom of Devavardhana, the kingdom of Kāśī, and the kingdom of Campā. All such kings as these should receive, uphold, and practice the Prajñāpāramitā.”
The commentary states:

"Entrusting [the teachings] to various kings so that they may uphold them, etc., ensures that the Honored One establishes the True Dharma (Saddharma) such that it shall forever be free from all difficulties.
The sixteen great nations listed herein differ slightly from those in the older versions of the sutra.

This differs from the Sanskrit pronunciation found in the sixteenth fascicle of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*, "The Moon-Treasury Section," and in the one hundred twenty-fourth fascicle of the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*; they cannot be reconciled.
From this point, the second [section] concerning the great assembly’s expression of astonishment:
The Sūtra says:
At that time, the great assembly, including the asuras and others, having heard the Buddha’s account of these various calamities, their body hair stood on end, and they cried out in a loud voice:
"I vow that in the future I shall not be born in that land.
The commentary states:
"The 'great assembly' at that time" refers to the collective.
The phrase "asuras and so forth" refers to specific categories.
"Various calamities" refers to the seven disasters and the like.
Because the times are turbid and evil, and because the causes of the seven disasters and so forth increase due to unwholesome karma.
Regarding those who do not take birth there, there are two meanings:
first, through the skillful means of great compassion, they destroy the aspiration for birth; second, due to the inferiority of their karmic retribution, they truly have no desire for birth.
From this, thirdly, all kings obtain benefit.

Sūtra: At that time, the sixteen kings immediately relinquished their royal thrones to practice the path of renunciation; they perfected the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and the ten spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), and attained the patience of subduing (*dharmanidhyānakṣānti*), the patience of faith (*adhimukticānti*), and the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*).
The commentary states:
Regarding the relinquishing of the royal throne, there are those who truly renounce their position and follow the path of monastic ordination;
there are also those who, because they have abandoned the prideful mind of royalty, give rise to the bodhicitta and thereby enter the way of monasticism.
The remaining eight superior [qualities] and so forth are fully as described previously.
The third major section concerns the benefits obtained from hearing the Dharma.
This is divided into two parts:
Furthermore, first, the great assembly obtained benefit.
The Sūtra says:

At that time, the entire great assembly of humans and devas, asuras, and others, scattered mandārava flowers, mañjūṣaka flowers, vārṣika flowers, and sumanā flowers as offerings to the Buddha; according to their respective dispositions, they attained the three gates of liberation, the emptiness of persons, the emptiness of phenomena, and the factors of enlightenment.
The commentary states:
"At that time, all those who were equal" refers to the assembly of listeners.
The first two refer to the flowers of the devas in heaven; the latter two refer to the flowers among human beings.
If these are actual flowers, they should be understood in full according to the text;
if they are manifested through transformation, they should be known by analogy with what precedes.
"According to their spiritual lineage" refers to the lineages of the three vehicles.
The attainment of the three gates of liberation and the realization of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) is common to all three vehicles.
The statement regarding the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) pertains exclusively to the Mahāyāna.
As for the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharmas*), these likewise pertain to all three vehicles, as detailed previously.
However, regarding those who attain the fruits of the three vehicles through the Dharma of Prajñā, as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, fascicle 593, the Bodhisattva Suvīra said:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion for us, will fully expound for us the realm and wisdom of the Tathāgata."
If there are classes of sentient beings whose nature is determined for the Śrāvaka Vehicle, having heard this Dharma, they will swiftly realize their own stage of outflowlessness (*anāsrava*).
Those whose nature is determined for the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, having heard this Dharma, will swiftly attain liberation by relying upon their own vehicle.
Those who are fixed in the nature of the Unsurpassed Vehicle, having heard this Dharma, will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Even those whose natures are not yet fixed among the three vehicles, having heard this Dharma, will swiftly give rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
Thus, the Dharma of Prajñā is not solely for the Mahāyāna, as it also enables those of the two vehicles to attain their own respective fruits.
This is the second section, concerning the benefits obtained by Bodhisattvas.
This passage is further divided into two parts:
Furthermore, regarding the first [stage], "Attaining Various Supreme Patiences," the Sūtra states:

"Immeasurable and incalculable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas scattered *gandhamūta* flowers and *padma* flowers as an offering to the Buddha; immeasurable samādhis all became manifest before them, and they attained the stage of compliance with patience (*ānulomikī kṣānti*) and the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)."
The commentary states:
"Bodhisattvas" refers to their great multitude, numbering in the infinite.
The scattering of lotus flowers in two colors, such as red and crimson, and the terms "samādhi" and "patience," are explained as previously described.
From this, secondly, regarding manifesting the body to attain Buddhahood, the Sūtra states:

"Immeasurable and innumerable Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas attained as many gates of samādhi as there are grains of sand in the Ganges; they realized the equality of the ultimate and the conventional, possessed unimpeded analytical knowledge, constantly gave rise to great compassion, and extensively benefited sentient beings across worlds as numerous as the atoms within a hundred trillion asaṃkhyeya Buddha-fields, manifesting their bodies to attain Buddhahood."
The commentary states:
"Immeasurable and so forth" clarifies the vastness of the bodhisattva.
"Samādhis as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River" clarifies the abundance of samādhis.
Regarding "the equality of the ultimate and the conventional": this distinguishes the objects of the truths and clarifies the possession of virtuous qualities through compassion.
Because one attains Buddhahood in every dust mote and land to extensively benefit and bring joy [to all], everyone who hears what has been previously taught shall obtain benefit.
Chapter Eight: Entrustment (Parindana-parivarta). This is the third major section, clarifying the *pratyāmnāya* (circulation) portion. To explain its purpose:
the preceding section extensively elucidated correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*), while the following section reveals the depth of compassion (*karuṇā*).

Although the Buddha’s wisdom and compassion are constantly uninterrupted, according to the sequence of the text, there is a partial emphasis on one or the other; this is because the following section explains various admonitions.

Regarding the title of the chapter: "zhù" (嘱) means entrustment, and "lèi" (累) means repeated accumulation; because they bear the Buddha’s repeated accumulation [of teachings], it is called "Entrustment and Accumulation" (Zhulei).
Furthermore, he entrusted this Dharma to the various kings, charging them to propagate it extensively so that the lineage of the Buddha would not be severed.
He also charged them with the Prajñāpāramitā to ensure its transmission through successive generations, thereby eliminating calamities and bringing benefit and happiness to sentient beings.

As in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, where the entrustment is made to the śrāvakas, and in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, where it is entrusted to the bodhisattvas; the benefit conferred through the gathering of those with specific capacities differs according to these distinctions.

This ensures that the Three Jewels will endure for a long time; it cannot be established by anyone other than a king. Since this fulfills what the host requested, the entrustment is made to no one else.
To analyze the text by its divisions, there are three main sections:
first, the designation of the Dharma to be entrusted; second, the extensive explanation of various admonitions; and third, the inquiry into the name and the practice thereof.
The first section on the entrustment of the Dharma is further divided into two parts.
First, regarding the initial [part], which marks the time of the entrustment of the Dharma: what is its meaning?
Sūtra: The Buddha addressed King Prasenajit:

"I now exhort you all: after my parinirvāṇa, when the True Dharma is about to perish—after fifty years, five hundred years, and five thousand years—there will be no Buddha, Dharma, or Saṅgha. This sūtra and the Three Jewels are entrusted to the various kings to establish and protect."
The commentary states:
"Now, 'to admonish you'—the term 'admonition' (诫) refers to instruction (教诫), in the sense of a formal injunction.
What distinguishes this from the other precepts is that these precepts follow the movement of the mind, arising through meditative concentration (定) and the Path (道)."
The precept that does not follow the mind is superior because it arises from intentional vows.

Regarding these admonitions herein, out of the Buddha’s great compassion, fearing that after his parinirvāṇa the True Dharma might vanish and that the ten non-virtuous actions of sentient beings might increase, leaving them to wander in saṃsāra without protection, he admonished kings and others to establish [these teachings].
Furthermore, it is admonished that both ordinary beings and sages must maintain and protect [the teachings], so that no calamities shall ever arise within the borders of any nation.
This is because the sutras and other scriptures state that there is nothing not encompassed [by this].
As for the "last five" periods and so forth, these refer to the times of the True Dharma (*saddharma*), the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpaka-dharma*), and the Final Dharma (*paścima-dharma*).

As stated in the lower fascicle of the *Mahāyāna-saṃbhava-sūtra*: "The Tathāgata manifests his descent from Tuṣita Heaven, and so forth, up to the sustaining of all true Dharma, all semblance Dharma, and all declining Dharma; such transformative activities are all the Nirmāṇakāya."

Furthermore, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-śāstra* (or *Samantapāsādikā*) states: "During the first millennium, if the disciples practice with diligence and vigor, they will attain the fruit of Arhatship.
During the second millennium, they will attain the third fruit."
In the third millennium, one attains the second fruit;
in the fourth millennium, one attains the first fruit.
From this point onward shall be my period of the Final Dharma (mofa).

According to the treatise, during the period of the True Dharma (Saddharma), many attain the fruit of No-more-learning (aśaikṣa); during the period of the Semblance Dharma (Pratirūpakadharma), one attains the first three fruits; and during the period of the Final Dharma (Paścimadharma), one does not attain the fruits of the Path.

Furthermore, according to the *Separate Record*, the True Dharma (Saddharma) lasts for one thousand years, the Semblance Dharma (Saddharmapratirūpaka) for one thousand years, and the Final Dharma (Antardharma) for ten thousand years.
Regarding these three distinct periods: that which possesses the teaching, the practice, and the realization of the fruit is called the True Dharma;
that which possesses the teaching and the practice but lacks the realization of the fruit is called the Semblance Dharma.
When there is only the teaching, but neither practice nor realization, it is called the Dharma-ending age (*mappō*).
Yet, while both the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* speak of five hundred years, this text speaks of fifty; what is the intended meaning of this?
As explained in the *Dharmasthitinirdeśa-sūtra*, this is illustrated by dividing [a lifespan] into one hundred parts and taking the latter fifty to represent the stage of decline.
It is like a person of a hundred years of age: the final fifty years are used as a metaphor for the Dharma, as they gradually lead toward deterioration.
Because the previous era was one of excellence, it was not difficult to establish [the teachings]; however, due to the subsequent degenerate age, all were entrusted [to others].

Furthermore, as stated in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, the Sarvāstivāda school asserts that the True Dharma will endure for five hundred years; thus, although the Eight Respectful Precepts (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*) were taught, they were not put into practice.
The Mahāsāṃghika school maintains that the True Dharma will endure for a thousand years; it is not the case that it will cease to be practiced entirely, for there will still be those who practice it.
Although there are these two textual accounts, the majority rely on the latter.

Furthermore, the *Dharmasthiti-sūtra* states: "Each of the sixteen Arhats, leading immeasurable retinues, when the human lifespan gradually increases to seventy thousand years, shall, by the power of their original vows, construct stūpas for the Buddha using the seven precious gems, and the relics of Śākyamuni will naturally flow into the stupas."

Subsequently, the reliquary stūpas of the Buddha all sank into the earth until they reached the adamantine layer (*vajra-maṇḍala*). At that time, the various arhats manifested fire to cremate their own bodies and entered parinirvāṇa.
Thereafter, seven koṭis of pratyekabuddhas appeared in the world to transform sentient beings.
"When the lifespan of the Perfect One gradually increases and decreases until it reaches eighty thousand years, they will all simultaneously enter parinirvāṇa without remainder.
Thereafter, Maitreya Buddha will appear in the world.

Furthermore, according to the *Padmavadana Sūtra*, at the time when the Buddha-dharma is finally extinguished, the Tathāgata’s śarīra will sink into the dragon palace; when the Dharma in the dragon palace is extinguished, it will sink into the adamantine limit (*vajraprakṣara*).
Subsequently, for seven days and seven nights, heaven and earth were pitch black. A voice from the sky addressed the non-Buddhists, saying:
"The Dharma of the śramaṇa Gautama has now been extinguished.
We shall now be able to teach and transform all sentient beings throughout the entire dharma-realm."
Having spoken these words, his body immediately sank into the Avīci Hell.
Subsequently, Maitreya Buddha appeared in the world.

As for the absence of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha: even if a river has little water, it may still be called "non-existent"; therefore, the Sūtra was entrusted based on the aforementioned three absences.
If there were nothing at all, what would there be to entrust?
From this point, the second [section] explains the practice.
The Sūtra says:

"Now my fourfold assembly of disciples receive, uphold, read, and recite [this teaching], understanding its principles and extensively proclaiming the essentials of the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, causing them to practice so as to transcend birth and death."
The commentary states:
Regarding the "four assemblies," there are two each for the ordained and the laity as mentioned above.
Regarding "renunciation," the cultivation of the three vehicles all leads to transcendence from birth and death.
From this point, the second section extensively explains the various admonitions.
This is divided into three parts:
first, the extensive explanation of the various admonitions; second, the respectful acceptance by the kings; and third, the lamentation of the great assembly.
First, the various admonitions are clarified; the text is divided into seven parts:
the first is the admonition against self-reliance and its resulting destruction.
This section is further divided into three parts:
Furthermore, first, the initial establishment of the person is indicated in the Sūtra:
"Great King!..."
"In the future age of the five turbidities, all kings, princes, and ministers, relying on their own high status and nobility, will destroy my teaching.
The commentary explains:

regarding the "five turbidities," according to the twelfth fascicle of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, they are the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*), the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*), the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*), the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*), and the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*).

Regarding what is called "turbidity" (*kaṣāya*), as the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "When the end of the kalpa is approaching, lifespan and other qualities become base and inferior, like dregs and filth; therefore, they are described as turbidities."

The *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Right Reasoning), fascicle 32, states: "Because they are extremely base and lowly, because they ought to be abandoned, and because they are like dregs and filth, they are called 'turbidities' (*kaṣāya*)."
The general statement "five" is an explanation by way of enumeration (*saṃkhyā-vyākhyā*).
To explain the specific names, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (44) states: "First is the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*), as in the present time when life is short."
Second is the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*), because as beings gradually enter the intermediate eons of the three calamities, their material requisites are diminished.

Third is the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*), because sentient beings for the most part associate with what is contrary to the Dharma and are tormented by greed, hatred, delusion, and so forth.
Fourth is the defilement of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*), because for the most part sentient beings destroy the True Dharma and increase the five views through false investigations.
Fifth is the defilement of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*), because for the most part sentient beings do not recognize their parents, do not perceive fear, and increase all manner of evils.

Regarding this sequence: life-span and the requisites for existence constitute dull or sharp karmic activity; because they depend upon suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*), they are categorized as results, conditions, and causes.
As stated in the *Siddhi-sthāna* (The Section on Establishment): "Dull or sharp karmic activity brings about internal and external results, depending on their antidotes and their abandonment."
Regarding the "five aggregates": life has the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) as its basis, and consciousness as its essential nature.
Sentient beings in the *kalpa*-defilement have the aggregates (*skandha*) as their essential nature.
Afflictions and views have mental factors (*caitta*) as their essential nature.
One type consists of four manifest [defilements], with the five aggregates as its substance.

As for the reason for establishing this, the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "Is it not the case that the three turbidities of lifespan, the eon, and sentient beings are mutually inseparable? Furthermore, the turbidity of views has afflictions as its very substance."

The five [signs] would not be established; while it is indeed logically so, they are nonetheless presented in this sequence to manifest the extreme intensification of the five types of decay. What are these five?
First, the decay of lifespan, because the duration of time is extremely short.
Second is the decline of material requisites, because they lack luster;
third is the decline of wholesome qualities, because one takes delight in unwholesome conduct;
fourth is the decline of tranquility, because mutual opposition leads to clamor and contention.
"Because the five [corruptions] cause the degeneration of the physical basis, it is not a vessel for supramundane merit.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Due to the first two corruptions, lifespan and material requisites are extremely diminished."

Due to the next two corruptions (*kaṣāya*), wholesome qualities (*kuśalapakṣa*) decline: because people delight in self-inflicted suffering, or because they impair the virtues of both householders and renunciants.
Due to the final corruption, one's own person declines, in terms of physical stature, complexion, strength, mindfulness, wisdom, diligence, valor, and freedom from disease.

Regarding this antidote: because one gives rise to various right views through the three roots of goodness and cultivates the fruits of the ten virtuous actions, which are supreme and wondrous, it is as analyzed in the regular [commentary].
"All kings" refers to all the kings within Jambudvīpa.
The princes and ministers are as explained in the text.

It means that these three individuals, possessing sovereign power and influence, received the entrustment from afar to establish the True Dharma; yet, failing to establish it, they relied instead on their own pride and noble status, and thus brought about its destruction.
From this, the second section clarifies what is contrary to the Dharma.
The Sūtra says:

"He openly established restrictive rules, forbidding my disciples—the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs—from leaving the household life to practice the Right Path, and likewise forbidding them from constructing Buddha-stūpas or images."
"A white-robed layperson sits upon a high seat while a bhikṣu stands on the ground; this is no different from the conduct of soldiers or slaves.
The commentary explains:
"To 'restrain my disciples' means not to allow them to leave the household life [as ordained]."
Those who practice the Right Path refer to practitioners of the dhūta ascetic virtues and the like.
Those who construct Buddha-stūpas and images refer to those who manufacture Buddha-images and stūpa-images.
"White-robed ones on high seats" refers to laypeople and monastics sitting on seats of varying heights.
These two are contrary to the Dharma, as is fully evident from the analogy.
From this, the third [section] concludes the clarification that it will not be long. Sūtra:
"One should know that at such a time, the Dharma will not long remain.
The commentary states:
Because of this initial [decline], there will be no transmitters whatsoever.
Because of the latter five [causes], existence does not endure for long.
This is followed by the second admonition concerning the destruction of the land.
The text is divided into three parts:
Furthermore, first, the initial [section] indicates the person who is capable of exercising restraint.
The Sūtra says:
“Great King!...”

"The causes and conditions for the destruction of the kingdom were all created by you yourself; relying on your own power, you have restrained the fourfold assembly and prevented them from practicing merit.
The commentary explains:

"Restraining the practice of the three trainings" refers to training in precepts, concentration, and wisdom; "restraining the practice of offerings" refers to obstructing the performance of true meritorious deeds.
From here, the second [section] clarifies what is not the Dharma.
The Sūtra says:

“When various evil bhikṣus accept individual invitations, and their acquaintances and fellow bhikṣus become of one mind, mutually affectionate and gathering together to seek merit—this is the dharma of external paths; it is by no means my teaching.”
"The common people suffer from pestilence and immeasurable hardships.
The commentary states:
To invite [monks] individually and to use hand-clapping [as a signal] is as reprehensible as the practices of non-Buddhists.

Because the monastic community failed to maintain proper discipline, thereby creating such unlawful conditions that disturbed the true cause [of the Dharma], they prohibited the cultivation of meritorious deeds as a cause for unwholesomeness; consequently, malevolent spirits and dragons wrought various sufferings and calamities.
From this, the third section concludes by clarifying the destruction.
The Sūtra states:
"One should know that at that time the land will be destroyed."
The commentary states:
This is fully explained according to the text.
From here follows the third [section]: the admonition that the Dharma will not long endure after its extinction.
The text is divided into three parts;
first, the initial section identifies the person who performs the action. Sūtra:
"Great King! In the final age of the Dharma, kings, ministers, and the fourfold assembly of disciples will each act contrary to the Dharma. Explanation:
This is the general heading.
Second, from here on, the text clarifies what is not the Dharma.
The Sūtra says:
"Unjustly attributing various faults to the Buddha’s teachings, they bind monks with what is neither Dharma nor Vinaya, like prisoners in a jail.
The commentary explains:
Those who possess virtue and rely upon it, practicing according to the instructions, are unjustly accused and illegally detained, just like prisoners in a jail.
From this, the third section concludes by clarifying that [the Dharma] will not remain for long.
The Sūtra states:
"One should know that at that time, the extinction of the Dharma will be near."
The commentary states: This refers to "bondage" (saṃyojana).
From this fourth [section] onward, it concerns how results are experienced in accordance with their causes.
This section is divided into three parts:
first, identifying those who destroy themselves; second, the retribution obtained through unrighteousness; and third, providing an analogy to explain this.
Within the first part, there are further two sub-sections:
Furthermore, first, the sūtra identifies those who destroy themselves:
"Great King!..."

After my parinirvāṇa, the fourfold assembly of disciples, as well as all kings, princes, and officials, who are the ones meant to uphold and protect the Triple Gem, will instead bring about its destruction themselves.
The commentary states:
"The fourfold assembly of disciples" refers to the community that sustains and maintains [the Dharma].
"Kings and their hundred officials" refers to the community that establishes protection.
The teaching relies upon these two to abide in the world, for without being upheld and protected, it would perish.
From this, the second point raises an analogy to reveal the fault.
The Sūtra says:
"The worms within a lion's body eat the lion's own flesh; they are not external parasites.
The commentary states:
"Regarding 'the worms within a lion's body,' as the *Padmavaktra-sūtra* records, the Buddha told Ānanda:"
"For example, when a lion dies, no sentient beings, whether of water or land, dare to eat its flesh.
Only the various worms that naturally arise within the lion's own body will consume the lion's meat."
"Ānanda! My Buddha-dharma cannot be destroyed by others; it is because the evil bhikṣus within my own Dharma destroy it themselves.
Just as that sutra used the analogy of the renunciants alone, this sutra fully clarifies that the fourfold assembly is unable to practice protection, for the analogy is the same in both cases.
From this, secondly, regarding the retribution obtained for violating the Dharma, it is divided into three parts:

first, retribution experienced in the present life (dr̥ṣṭadharmavedanīya); second, retribution experienced in the next life (upapadyavedanīya); and third, retribution experienced in subsequent lives (aparaparyāyavedanīya).
The first section further divides into two parts;
first, the initial part clarifies various evils.
The Sūtra states:

"Those who destroy my Dharma shall incur great transgression; the True Dharma will decline and thin out, the people will lack upright conduct, and all manner of evils will gradually increase. Their lifespans will diminish day by day; there will be no more filial sons, the six types of kin will live in discord, and the devas and nāgas will offer no protection."
The commentary states:
"Those who destroy my Dharma and so forth" consists of two phrases that serve as the heading.
"The True Dharma declines and thins out" and so forth clarifies the practice of the heterodox.
Regarding the phrase "various evils gradually increase" and so forth: it means that as unwholesome conduct gradually increases, the lifespan becomes shortened.
Regarding the phrase "there are no longer filial sons" and so forth: it means that within the family there are no filial sons, and the six types of kinship relations are in disharmony.
"Those whom the devas and nāgas do not protect" means that the eight classes of devas and nāgas abandon them and depart.
This second [point] clarifies the arising of calamities and anomalies.
The Sūtra says:
"Evil ghosts and evil dragons come daily to inflict harm; calamities and strange portents succeed one another as disasters run rampant.
The commentary states:
"Evil ghosts" refers to pestilence and epidemics; "evil dragons" refers to droughts, floods, and unseasonable winds and rains.
"Calamities and portents occurring in succession" means that various hardships arise in competition.

Regarding the terms "longitudinal" and "transverse": north and south are longitudinal, while east and west are transverse; this clarifies that there are disasters and difficulties in all four directions.
From this, the second [section] clarifies the retribution of the next life.
The Sūtra says:
"They shall fall into the hells, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts."
The commentary states:

Regarding "destined to fall" and so forth, when one performs unwholesome karma of superior, middling, or inferior grades, one undergoes the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) within the three evil destinies.
Following this, the third section clarifies those [karmas] that yield results in subsequent lives.
Sūtra: “If one obtains a human birth, one will be poor, lowly, and base, with incomplete sense faculties. Commentary:
This clarifies the retribution in a subsequent life.
From here, the third section provides an analogy to explain and establish this point.
The Sūtra says:
"Just as a shadow follows a form and an echo responds to a sound, and just as when a person writes at night the characters remain even after the fire is extinguished,
so too is the karmic retribution for destroying the Dharma."
The commentary states:
"As a shadow follows a form" means that the shadow and the body exist together; this is a metaphor for accordance with the present life.
"As an echo responds to a sound"—when the sound ceases, the echo responds; this is a metaphor for accordance with future rebirth.

It is like a person writing at night whose characters remain even after the fire has been extinguished: the fire is a metaphor for the karma performed, and the characters are a metaphor for the perfuming (vāsanā).

The simultaneous appearance of both the fire and the characters is a metaphor for the simultaneous manifestation of the single entity—both the present [karma] and the seed; this is cited to illustrate that which is not seen by pointing to the limits of what one can perceive.
Although the karmic action of fire has ceased, the seeds of its syllabic nature do not perish; they will inevitably ripen as favorable subsequent retributions, whether near or distant.
Furthermore, how many types of present existence are there, and what kind of karma definitively brings them about?
The superior causes for defiled and wholesome [states] are as previously analyzed.
Following this, the fifth section concerns the Buddha-dharma not being long-lasting.
This passage is divided into three parts:
Furthermore, first is the person who establishes the Dharma through regulation.
The Sūtra says:
“Great King!...”
"In all future ages, [this shall apply to] all kings, princes, and ministers.
The commentary states:
"This refers to those who establish the Dharma."
From this second point, its illegality is clarified.
The Sūtra states:

“They arbitrarily establish registries for my disciples, appointing officials and masters to oversee the positions of Great and Small Monastic Chiefs (Sengtong), and employ them in unreasonable service.”
The commentary states:

Among those who have left home in the Western Regions, there are no official registers established, nor are there any officials in charge; within the Sangha, there is no centralized administration whatsoever.
Those who are subjected to unreasonable labor service are treated the same as the secular population regarding corvée labor.
From this point, the third [section] concerns the Dharma not remaining for long.
The Sūtra states:
"It should be known that at that time, the Buddha-dharma will not remain for long."
The commentary states:
This is as explained in the text.
From this point begins the sixth section: the prohibitions against accepting heterodox and perverse teachings.
The text is divided into three parts;
first, the initial section designates the reliance upon the Dharma and the person. Sūtra:
“Great King! In future ages, all kings and the fourfold assembly of disciples shall rely upon the path constantly practiced by all Buddhas of the ten directions to establish and propagate it.”
The commentary states:
Establishing the three trainings is itself the eternal Way.
From this second point onward, its non-Dharma nature is clarified.
The text is further divided into two parts.
First, the initial section clarifies the arising of what is not the Dharma.
The Sūtra states:
"Furthermore, wicked bhikṣus, seeking fame and profit, do not rely upon my Dharma; they speak of their own faults before kings, creating conditions for the destruction of the Dharma.
The commentary states:
"Not relying upon my Dharma" means that anything outside of the Three Trainings is entirely not the Buddha-Dharma.
The violation of the Dharma in the vicinity should be understood through these matters.
From this, secondly, the rules for transgressions are clarified. Sūtra:
"The king did not discern [the truth], but believed and accepted these words, arbitrarily establishing restrictive laws that do not rely on the Buddha’s precepts.
The commentary states:
According to the various Vinaya schools, one should practice in accordance with the Dharma as established by the Buddha.
That which the Buddha has not prohibited should not be arbitrarily prohibited; to prohibit it would be incorrect.
From this, the third section concludes the clarification that [the teaching] will not endure for long. Sūtra:
"One should know that at such a time, the Dharma will not long remain.
The commentary states:
This is entirely as the text says.
From here follows the seventh admonition on personally causing the destruction of one's own state.
The text is divided into three parts;
first, the initial section identifies the person who acts upon themselves.
Sūtra: “Great King! In a future age, there will be kings, ministers, and the fourfold assembly of disciples.”
The commentary states:
This identifies the person.
From this point, secondly, it clarifies what is not the Dharma.
The Sūtra says:

"One creates the causes and conditions for the destruction of the Dharma and the ruin of the nation through one's own actions; one receives the retribution for this oneself. It is not the fault of the Buddha-dharma. The devas and nāgas abandon the land, and my turbidity increases further."
The commentary states:
"One who personally destroys the Dharma" refers to the fourfold assembly's inability to practice in accordance with the teachings and the Dharma.
"Causes and conditions for the destruction of the state" refers to kings and ministers themselves failing to uphold what is correct and establish the True Dharma.
These two support one another; as the True Dharma disappears, devas and nāgas no longer provide protection because the five turbidities increase.
From this second point, the enumeration of faults is inexhaustible. Sūtra:
"If explained in full detail, it would not be exhausted even at the end of an eon.
The commentary states:

"This concludes, in the near term, that the defilements of this degenerate age are inexhaustible; in the distant sense, it concludes that the six aforementioned categories are likewise inexhaustible."
From this point, the second section concerns how all the kings reverently received [the news].
This is divided into two parts;
first, the initial section concerning the lamentation of all the kings.

Sūtra: At that time, when the sixteen great kings heard these various admonitions concerning the future, they wept and wailed so bitterly that their voices shook the trichiliocosm; heaven and earth grew dark and dim, and no light appeared.
The commentary states:
The various kings wept with such intensity that they shook the great trichiliocosm; the sun and moon did not appear, which signifies utter darkness.
From this point, the second section follows the teaching with reverent acceptance.

Sūtra: At that time, each of the kings sincerely received and upheld the Buddha’s words, resolving not to restrict the fourfold assembly from leaving home to study the Path, but rather to act in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching.
Explanation:
This is fully explained in the text.
From this point follows the third section: the lamentation of the great assembly.
The Sūtra says:
At that time, a great multitude as numerous as the sands of the Ganges all sighed together, saying:
"At such a time, the world is empty and void; this is an age without a Buddha."
The commentary states:
This is an expression of lamentation for an evil age, wherein right wisdom has perished and the preservation of the Teaching has vanished; thus, there is no Buddha.
From this point follows the third inquiry, titled "Practice and Observation."
This section is divided into two parts:
first, the inquiry concerning the title of the sutra; second, the explanation of its practice.
Within the first part, there are five further sections:
Furthermore, at the beginning, the second benevolent king poses a question.
The sutra states:
At that time, King Prasenajit addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What should this sutra be named?
How should we uphold it?”
The commentary states: "To 'understand' means to receive and uphold [the teaching] upon hearing its name.
From this point, the second section follows, wherein the World-Honored One provides the answer.
Sūtra: The Buddha addressed the Great King:
"This sūtra is named the *Benevolent Kings' Protection of the Nation Prajñāpāramitā*."
It may also be called the "Ambrosial Medicine of the Dharma"; if there are those who ingest and practice it, they will be able to cure all ailments.
The commentary states:
Regarding the title of this sutra, the first part refers to the "Inquiry of the Benevolent Kings," which is named after its petitioner.
Next, based on its qualities, it is shown that it can cure the illness of birth and death.
If even deep-seated karmic burdens can be dispelled, how much more so minor and superficial calamities, which would surely be extinguished?
This concludes the third section, clarifying the merit of the sutra.
Sūtra: “Great King! All the merits of the Prajñāpāramitā are like space; they cannot be measured.”
The commentary states:
Following the meanings of these various phrases, they are as unfathomable as space.
From this fourth [point], one is able to protect the king and his ministers.
Sūtra: "If there are those who receive, uphold, read, and recite this, the merit they obtain will be able to protect the Benevolent Kings and all sentient beings. Explanation:
The power of the sutra is profound and subtle; according to one’s reading and its upholding, the majestic light of great compassion is equal, without distinction of high or low.
From this, the fifth analogy clarifies the act of receiving and upholding. Sutra:
"It is like a wall and also like a crumbling rampart;
therefore, you all should receive and uphold it.
The commentary explains:
Protecting the family and protecting the nation are two metaphors for upholding [the teaching].
This is the second section: the Great Assembly’s Reverent Upholding.
The Sūtra says:

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, Maitreya, Siṃhanāda, and immeasurable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; Śāriputra, Subhūti, and immeasurable śrāvakas; immeasurable devas and humans of the desire realm; bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās; and the entire great assembly including asuras—having heard what the Buddha preached, were all greatly rejoiced, and they faithfully accepted and practiced it.
The commentary states:
The great assembly, having heard the Dharma, rejoiced and practiced it with zeal.

Liang Ben sighed that we dwell in the age of the semblance dharma (*xiangji*), where the Sage is no longer seen in person; yet, he joyfully cultivates the profound movement of the Way and sorrowfully upholds its lingering radiance.

The old commentaries have been transmitted for a long time, filling every corner of the realm; now that the Great Tang reigns over the calendar and its brilliance shines upon the four seas, this sutra is being translated anew, and an imperial decree has been issued to provide a commentary.

I, Liang Ben, am but one of the lowest among the monastic assembly; how could I dare claim to have mastered the "trap and snare" of the teachings? Nevertheless, I shall unroll the threads of the sutras and let my humble glow assist the sun. Having consulted the ancient tracks and approaching the task with evening vigilance as if standing over a deep abyss, my words and meanings are sparse and coarse, which only increases my shame and trepidation.
I entreat the eminent masters to examine and correct this in detail.
Having gathered the essential points from the sūtras and śāstras, I have appended these praises to the wondrous and inconceivable Prajñāpāramitā.
May the merit of this small good deed be bestowed upon all sentient beings, and may we together swiftly ascend to unsurpassed enlightenment.

The *Commentary on the Benevolent Kings Sūtra*, Scroll Lower, Part Three, concludes here. The Dharma Master Zhiju was of lofty brilliance and his literary peaks rose in exquisite distinction. Having personally relied upon the Sanskrit manuscripts to propagate and expound the subtle words, he probed the profound mysteries of the True Doctrine and composed this formal commentary. It opens the secret treasury of the Tathāgata and reveals the ferrying ford for those lost among all beings. Stringing together jade and pearls, it probes the deep and reaches the far; having read and reviewed it repeatedly, I consider it remarkably precise and detailed. May it be transmitted to monasteries to serve forever as a treasure of the Dharma.
The śramaṇa Liangbei submitted this statement:

I have reverently received the imperial decree of the eleventh day of the second month of this year, ordering me to reside within the palace at the Southern Peach Garden to compile a commentary on the newly translated *Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

I, a humble monk of meager learning, fear that I may not be worthy of Your Majesty’s intent. Thus, I have cleansed my mind and aroused my thoughts, knocking upon the silence to seek its resonance. My illumination begins with the Celestial Words (the Buddha’s teachings), and my reliance for empowerment is placed upon the power of the Buddha. All is based upon the sūtras and śāstras to expound the True Vehicle (*samyak-yāna*). This is like gathering jade from Mount Kunlun or receiving great rivers into the vast ocean; it is like fire produced from wood shining together with the seven luminaries, or consciousness transforming within wisdom, where the single mark of the essence shines equally. That which realizes the Way is the Dharma; that which carries the Dharma is the Sūtra; and that which explains the Sūtra is the Commentary (*ṭīkā*). To extensively deliver all beings is identical to the Great Pervasion (*mahā-saṃbheda*).

This *Bodhicitta* [text], in accordance with Your Majesty’s intent, has been carefully completed on the eighth day of this month. It consists of over ten thousand words and comprises three fascicles. I am personally ashamed that its execution reflects only my own meager views and its composition differs from Your Majesty’s sublime grace. Along with one fascicle of the ritual procedures for the recitation of *dhāraṇīs*, and one scroll of the *Record of the Imperial Audience* during the lecture on the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* at the Chengming Hall, I now submit them all together.
I, the humble dust [of the clergy], have received this profound discernment; my sense of awe and trepidation is beyond measure.
I respectfully submit this memorial to present it for Your Majesty’s perusal.
I, the śramaṇa Liangbei, speak with both sincere joy and sincere fear. Thus, I say.
On the eighth day of the eleventh month in the second year of the Yongtai era,
the śramaṇa Liangbei respectfully submitted this memorial in response to an imperial edict concerning internal cultivation.
